name: The Impossible Trinity
statement: A country can have any two of a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows, and its own monetary policy, but never all three.
meaning: The impossible trinity holds that a country cannot simultaneously maintain a fixed exchange rate, free movement of capital across its borders, and an independent monetary policy. It can secure at most two of the three; pursuing all three at once is impossible. A policymaker must therefore give up one corner to hold the other two, choosing which goal to sacrifice. The result is a foundational constraint on how open economies can manage their exchange rates, their capital accounts, and their control over domestic interest rates.
mechanism: The constraint works through capital flows and interest-rate arbitrage. With an open capital account, a central bank cannot both hold a fixed exchange rate and set domestic interest rates freely. If it pushes domestic rates below world rates, investors sell the domestic currency for higher-yielding foreign assets, creating depreciation pressure that forces the bank to intervene, spending reserves and adjusting rates to defend the peg. Defending the peg thus consumes monetary policy. Only by giving up one goal, floating the currency, controlling capital, or abandoning monetary independence, can the other two coexist.

examples.text: The United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada keep free capital movement and independent monetary policy, and pay for it by letting their exchange rates float.
Members of the euro chose a fixed rate among themselves plus free capital movement, surrendering national monetary independence to the European Central Bank, a textbook corner solution.
A country determined to hold both a peg and its own monetary policy must restrict the free flow of capital, as under the Bretton Woods system.

variants.name: The Mundell-Fleming model
variants.text: The underlying framework, developed independently by Robert Mundell and Marcus Fleming in the early 1960s, from which the trilemma is drawn; the 'trilemma' framing itself came later.

variants.name: Rey's dilemma
variants.text: Helene Rey's argument that a global financial cycle constrains national monetary policy whenever capital is mobile, regardless of the exchange-rate regime, so the choice collapses from a trilemma into a dilemma.

whyItMatters: It is foundational to international macroeconomics, structuring how economists and policymakers think about the choice of exchange-rate regime for any open economy. It clarifies the trade-offs behind the euro, the debates over capital controls, the design of the Bretton Woods system, and the acute tensions facing emerging markets that want stable pegs, open capital accounts, and domestic monetary control at once. By naming a hard limit, it disciplines expectations about what monetary and exchange-rate policy can jointly achieve.

working.text: when designing exchange-rate and monetary policy, accept that at most two of fixed rate, open capital, and monetary autonomy can be held together.
expect that with open capital markets, defending a peg will consume monetary policy through the pressure of cross-border flows.
interpret a country's exchange-rate arrangement as a decision about which corner of the trinity it has given up.

limits: It is a model-based proposition, not an empirical law, and its clean corners are idealisations. The real world offers intermediate regimes, managed floats, crawling pegs, partial or targeted capital controls, and sterilised intervention, that occupy the middle ground rather than pure corners. Capital controls are imperfect, often evaded, and introduce distortions, complicating the fixed-rate-plus-autonomy corner. The most prominent modern challenge is Helene Rey's argument that a floating exchange rate does not fully insulate monetary policy, because a global financial cycle constrains it whenever capital is mobile, turning the trilemma into a dilemma.
misreadings: It does not mean a country can have a little of all three; the strict proposition is a corner constraint, and intermediate regimes represent partial trade-offs, not an escape from it. A fixed exchange rate does not by itself cost a country its monetary independence; the binding condition is a fixed rate combined with open capital markets, since a peg plus capital controls can preserve autonomy. And a floating exchange rate does not guarantee full monetary independence, which is precisely the traditional claim that Rey's work disputes.
origin: Drawn from the Mundell-Fleming model developed independently by Robert Mundell (1963) and Marcus Fleming (1962); the 'trilemma' framing was developed and popularised later, notably by Maurice Obstfeld, Alan Taylor, and Paul Krugman in the 1990s, and challenged by Helene Rey in 2015.

sources.text: Impossible trinity, Wikipedia. — the three-way constraint, the arbitrage mechanism, the Mundell-Fleming origin, and Rey's dilemma critique.
